Believe it or not, a lot of thought was put in the way Congress is designed, and having a website based around ordinary people giving a popular vote would cause a ton of problems.

Firstly, the makeup of Congress is designed so that all states have a reasonable level of representation. Just having a website where everyone votes means that populous regions such as the East Coast would matter way more than rural ones, and this would result in a tyranny of the majority.

Secondly, if you have this style of democracy people are generally only going to vote on issues that they care about. For them to vote on everything, it would become a huge time commitment. You think someone who works 80 hours a week is going to take time and vote on something? These people who wouldn't have time to vote would risk being subjected to rules imposed on them by people who merely have more time--possibly because they're unemployed. The whole point of having a representative is so that you can have your interests protected when you don't have the time to engage in politics.

Thirdly, the reason Congressmen serve for terms is precisely so that they can sometimes do things which are unpopular when it's time to vote but proven correct at a later date. Giving everyone the power to vote creates an extreme moral hazard, and long-term collective action issues would never be addressed properly.

Fourthly, Congressmen have huge staff surrounding them to help them with their tasks. The most important duty of these staffers is to explain policy issues. A lay person just voting on a website most likely won't know diddly squat about most of the issues, and they won't be able to call on experts to help them.

Fifthly, Congress isn't just responsible for voting yea or nay on bills, they are also responsible for amending bills, creating budgets, and holding the power of the purse. Can you imagine trying to get a budget passed where every single person has a say in budget allocation? It would be impossible to allocate money in the specified manner required of Congress.

And lastly, Congress is also has the lesser known responsibility of hearing testimony to ensure that federal funds are being used properly. Just recently there was a hearing about Planned Parenthood to determine if federal funds were being used for abortions, and there was also a hearing recently to try to determine who in the EPA was responsible for the catastrophe at the Animas River. You really think average people would be willing to essentially engage in full time jury duty to fulfill this role?

And that's all assuming that the system is somehow impossibly secure.

Congress causes so many headaches for us that it's easy to think it's a broken system, but it's not as bad as people generally think. A few tweaks to things like campaign financing or gerrymandering would resolve most problems, but the only people with the power to change that also happen to be the ones that benefit from the status quo.

If you want an example of just how bad this system would be, just look at Greece's referendum. The country's economy is in the toilet, but when the people were asked if they would be willing to give up the government funded benefits that are causing the problems, the people still voted to stay the course on a doomed path.
